answer.answer:
Yes. # High-throughput screening of aluminum alloys for hot strength and creep

**Yes—but the demonstrated approaches are mostly separate pieces of the proposed workflow.** Researchers have obtained multiple elevated-temperature creep curves from individual additively manufactured (AM) aluminum specimens, measured hot indentation properties locally within an aluminum alloy, and tested four aluminum-based small-punch creep specimens simultaneously. I did **not** find a published demonstration that combines a *compositionally graded AM aluminum-alloy library* with systematic hot-hardness mapping or long-duration creep screening across its compositions. That is a search-limited finding, not proof that no such study exists. (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 3-5, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 2-3, shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4, michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 1-3)

The table separates experiments that actually measured aluminum at elevated temperature from composition-library studies conducted at room temperature and multi-specimen methods demonstrated on other metals.

| Paper / method | Material and measured temperature | Actual throughput and evidence | Boundary of applicability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Singh et al. (2022), DIC-augmented cantilever creep | LPBF AlSi10Mg; **250 °C**, 75–140 MPa | One beam supplies creep data at multiple stress-invariant locations; reported good agreement with uniaxial creep (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3) | Direct elevated-temperature AM-Al demonstration, but details here come from Kulkarni et al.’s 2023 description rather than the inaccessible original; one alloy, not a composition library |
| Kulkarni et al. (2023), DIC-augmented cantilever creep | LPBF A205 (Al–Cu–Mg–Ag–TiB₂); **200 °C** | **Two cantilever tests** covered 120–180 MPa and generated tensile and compressive curves at multiple locations; rates matched conventional uniaxial results below 170 MPa and were within a factor of two above it (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3, kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 5-7) | Strong direct validation for rapid creep characterization of one AM alloy; not simultaneous screening of multiple compositions |
| Krizik et al. (2024), small-punch creep | HITEMAL ultrafine-grained Al–Al₂O₃ composite; **573–673 K (300–400 °C)** | Four loading stages permitted **four discs to be tested simultaneously**; 8-mm-diameter × 0.5-mm discs, two creep replicates per condition; correlated with tensile creep at 573 K (krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 1-3, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 3-5) | Direct parallel aluminum SPCT, but one material; converting punch force/deflection rate to uniaxial stress/rate requires material-specific calibration, and deformation localized near radial fractures |
| Richter et al. (2008), hot-stage nanoindentation | Multicomponent Al–Ni–Si piston alloy; **300, 500 and 650 K** | Repeated indents mapped local phases and a within-grain Ni variation; Al₃Ni₂, Al₇Cu₄Ni and Al₂Cu showed phase-dependent hardness loss and indentation creep (richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 1-2, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 2-3, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 4-5) | Direct hot hardness/local-creep evidence, but the specially coarsened specimen was neither an AM library nor a systematic combinatorial composition gradient |
| Shen et al. (2025), diffusion-multiple nanoindentation creep | **12 Al–Mg–Si micro-alloys** in a 6016/Al–3Si/Al–1.2Mg/Al diffusion multiple; measurements at **room temperature** | Three repeats per composition; 15-mN indentation with a **900-s hold** after diffusion annealing and solution/aging treatments (shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4) | Genuine high-throughput composition screening, but not elevated-temperature testing—the 530–540 °C steps fabricated/heat-treated the library rather than setting the indentation temperature |

(2026), four specimens coupled in series with DIC | Commercial **316L stainless steel**, not aluminum; **650 °C**, 250–325 MPa | Four different cross-sections generated four stresses under one force; benchmarked against individual tests and delivered up to four creep tests in approximately the time of the slowest one (singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 1-3, singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 3-5, singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 10-11) | Demonstrates a transferable multi-specimen-frame concept, but provides no aluminum-alloy validation or compositional-library screen |

The method is DIC-augmented bending creep using a single beam, which generates multiple creep datasets in both tension and compression from sub-standard-sized samples. The approach was validated against conventional uniaxial creep: bending and uniaxial correlations showed an excellent match across 120–170 MPa, and the method was intended to avoid premature tertiary creep while estimating the creep stress exponent. At 200 °C, LPBF A205 exhibited minimum creep rates on the order of 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ s⁻¹ over 120–180 MPa. The reported strengthening mechanism is nano-scale Ω (Al-Cu-Ag-Mg) and θ′ (Al-Cu) precipitates pinning dislocations near grain-boundary precipitate-free zones. The excerpt does not provide the number of beam specimens, a composition library, individual test durations, or a detailed temperature matrix; therefore, this is a high-throughput geometry/method demonstration for one alloy rather than combinatorial alloy screening. It also reports that a cast 3 wt.% TiB2/Al-Cu-Mg-Ag counterpart had approximately threefold better creep resistance, providing a material comparison but not an alloy-library experiment.

contexts.context: This excerpt directly documents elevated-temperature, small-volume screening of one specific aluminum-based material: HITEMAL©, a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained Al metal-matrix composite stabilized and strengthened by a continuous in-situ amorphous Al2O3 skeletal network. Results were explicitly correlated with conventional uniaxial tensile-creep measurements, and the authors proposed correlation through a transition stress. HITEMAL© showed high apparent stress exponents and substantially higher creep performance than other powder-metallurgy Al alloys and composites under the tested conditions. Important limitations are stated: converting punch force and minimum deflection rate into equivalent uniaxial stress and creep rate is a major source of error, and standardized conversion procedures based largely on steels may not transfer reliably to new materials or metal-matrix composites. The discs also fractured by radial cracks at low deflection, with limited and localized creep deformation, so SPCT failure behavior may not represent extensive homogeneous creep. contexts.context: This excerpt does not demonstrate high-throughput screening of an aluminum alloy; it reports a stainless-steel method that may serve as a methodological comparator. The approach couples four 1/5-scale ASTM-E8 pin-loaded 316L stainless-steel specimens in series. Because the specimens have different cross-sectional areas, the same applied force produces different stresses in each specimen. Digital Image Correlation independently measures the strain of each specimen, overcoming the limitation that the creep frame monitors only the relative motion between the assembly endpoints. Validation used individual specimens as a benchmark and four coupled specimens under nominal stresses of 250, 275, 300, and 325 MPa at 650 °C. When one specimen fails, the test is paused, the failed specimen is removed, and testing resumes with the remaining specimens; cooling and removal require approximately 3–4 hours, with occasional additional overnight delay. The authors report that the four tests finish in nearly the time required by the slowest individual test, providing up to a fourfold increase in testing throughput. The excerpt therefore supplies evidence of simultaneous elevated-temperature creep testing and comparison with single-specimen tests, but it does not address AlSi10Mg, A205, HITEMAL, Al-Ni-Si, Al-Mg-Si diffusion multiples, alloy libraries, room-temperature indentation creep, or direct comparison with conventional uniaxial creep for aluminum.

contexts.context: Shen et al. demonstrate high-throughput screening of Al-Mg-Si deformation and indentation-creep behavior using a kinetic diffusion multiple (KDM), not elevated-temperature uniaxial creep. EPMA generated compositionally graded regions from a 6016/Al-3Si/Al-1.2Mg diffusion multiple, producing multiple ternary Al-Mg-Si material areas (MAs); the excerpt identifies at least MA#2, MA#9, and MA#10 but does not state the total number of compositions or specimens. Nanoindentation continuous-stiffness measurements and creep tests were performed at room temperature. The study evaluated pop-in behavior, indentation size effects, hardness, creep response, stress exponents, and activation volumes. Activation volumes ranged from 19 b3 to 142 b3: low values were associated with solute-atmosphere barriers, while high values indicated precipitate-cluster obstacles. MA#9, with Mg/Si atomic ratio approximately 0.75, showed minimal creep depth and a moderate activation volume of 44 b3. The conclusions report that composition and Mg/Si ratio alter dislocation activity, with precipitate hardening dominating pop-in suppression near Mg/Si ≈ 0.7–1.0. The excerpt provides no elevated test temperature, test duration, specimen count, direct comparison with conventional uniaxial creep, or explicit quantitative limitation beyond noting that direct evidence of dislocation nucleation was not observed. Thus, it is an alloy-library screening study based on room-temperature indentation creep rather than a high-temperature creep validation.

contexts.context: This excerpt directly demonstrates elevated-temperature, high-throughput creep screening for a single additively manufactured aluminum alloy: LPBF A205 (A20X), nominally Al-5.50Cu-3.68Ti-1.58B-0.61Ag-0.21Mg (wt.%). The method is a small-scale cantilever bending creep test augmented by digital image correlation (DIC), which measures the two-dimensional strain field. Testing was performed at 200°C, with reported minimum creep strain rates on the order of 10^-8–10^-6 s^-1 at stresses of 120–180 MPa. The study also used conventional ASTM E139-style uniaxial creep testing and explicitly established equivalence between uniaxial and bending creep. A key throughput advantage is that one bending specimen/test can produce both tension and compression creep curves, using small specimens, making the method potentially suitable for near-net-shape AM components and structure–property data generation. The excerpt does not state the number of bending or uniaxial specimens, test duration, or detailed quantitative agreement between the methods. It concerns elevated-temperature creep, not room-temperature indentation creep, and it is single-alloy testing rather than an alloy library or composition-gradient screening approach. The cited room-temperature indentation study of cast and AM A205 is mentioned only as prior work and should not be conflated with this 200°C high-throughput creep demonstration.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that Richter et al. examined individually pure and intermetallic phases in multi-component Al–Ni–Si piston alloys using hot-stage nanoindentation at room temperature, 500 K, and 650 K. They measured phase hardness and indentation/reduced modulus, finding that both generally decreased with increasing temperature, with phase-dependent rates. Higher Ni content in grains was associated with improved mechanical stability at elevated temperature. AFM was used to characterize indentation depth and pile-up, while FIB lift-out and TEM were used for site-specific examination of microstructural changes beneath indents. The article combined experiments with atomistic finite-element calculations for Si and Ni–Al systems over varying Ni contents and temperatures. The abstract reports little temperature-dependent mechanical change for Si between 300 and 650 K, whereas Al showed substantially increased plasticity at higher temperature and a transition from well-defined slip to viscous fluid-like atomic motion. It also studied dislocation and slip-band formation in Ni–Al systems. This excerpt does not identify the full phase list, specimen architecture or any composition-gradient/library design, nor does it provide quantitative hot-hardness or indentation-creep data. It likewise contains no information on direct combinatorial additive-manufactured Al-alloy hot-hardness studies or Singh 2026’s 316L multi-specimen creep frame.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns a 2025 high-throughput kinetic diffusion multiple (KDM) study of Al-Mg-Si alloys, not the 2008 Richter, Chen, and Smith hot-stage nanoindentation study of Al-Ni-Si alloys. It reports a 6016/Al-3Si/Al-1.2Mg/Al diffusion-multiple specimen that developed compositional and microstructural gradients extending over more than 1000 micrometers after diffusion annealing at 530 °C for 72 h. It finds that increasing Mg and Si suppresses pop-in events, with events nearly eliminated above 1.0 wt.% owing to solute–dislocation interactions. Indentation-size-effect analysis indicated maximum strengthening at an Mg-to-Si atomic ratio near 1 for fixed total solute content. Creep stress-exponent and activation-volume analysis attributed creep primarily to dislocation motion. contexts.context: This excerpt does not describe Richter, Chen, and Smith’s 2008 hot-stage nanoindentation study of multicomponent Al–Ni–Si alloys, nor does it provide evidence about Al-alloy combinatorial additive-manufacturing or diffusion-multiple measurements. Instead, it reports analogous elevated-temperature nanoindentation work on Ni-base superalloys and a combinatorial diffusion multiple. Testing was conducted from approximately 30°C to 400°C, including single-crystal CMSX-4 orientations and constituent alloys in a diffusion multiple. The graded chemistry across interdiffusion zones produced spatial changes in measured hardness and modulus. The authors emphasize that elevated-temperature creep during the dwell affects unloading compliance and must be corrected in the modified Oliver–Pharr analysis; otherwise, the modulus can be substantially overestimated. Creep displacement increased with temperature, while the creep displacement rate remained relatively constant during the dwell, with little evidence of accelerated primary creep. The excerpt also reports anomalous hot hardening in CMSX-4, attributed primarily to Kear–Wilsdorf locks and macro-kinks in the ordered γ′ precipitates, with cube slip becoming active at higher temperature. It contains no information on Singh 2026, a multi-specimen creep frame, or 316L. Figures are referenced in the source, but no image content is available here.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports hot-stage nanoindentation on a multicomponent Al–Ni–Si alloy at 300, 500, and 650 K, with comparison data for aluminium and single-crystalline silicon. The specimen contains relatively large grains—several tens of micrometres—selected so that repeated indents could be placed within individual grains. AFM imaging, EDX, and EBSD identified Al3Ni2, Al7Cu4Ni, and Al2Cu intermetallic phases, while a Ni-composition gradient within a grain was tracked. At fixed normal load, higher-Ni Al3Ni2 produced smaller indents, indicating greater hardness, whereas Al2Cu produced larger pits and lower hardness. The intermetallic hardnesses lay between those of aluminium and silicon. Aluminium showed the strongest temperature-related penetration increase and creep; the excerpt also states that plastic flow and creep were more pronounced in Al7Cu4Ni than Al3Ni2, with creep increasing in Al3Ni2 at 650 K. Generally, penetration depth increased strongly at 650 K, and hardness decreased with temperature; silicon fell from 11.1 GPa at 300 K to 9.2 GPa at 650 K. This excerpt does not provide evidence about direct Al-alloy combinatorial additive-manufacturing or diffusion-multiple hot-hardness measurements, nor about the cited Singh 2026 316L multi-specimen creep frame.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a high-throughput Al-Mg-Si composition-gradient study using a quadruple diffusion multiple (KDM), not the requested Richter, Chen, and Smith (2008) hot-stage study of Al-Ni-Si alloys. The KDM was fabricated from Al-1.2Mg, Al-3Si, 6016 alloy, and high-purity aluminum, diffusion-bonded at 540 °C, subsequently held at 530 °C for 72 h, quenched, and given solution/aging treatments at 530 °C for 30 min followed by 185 °C for 20 min. EPMA identified local Mg-Si compositions across the diffusion zones; twelve representative micro-alloys covered approximately 0.16–0.55 wt.% Mg and 0.18–0.85 wt.% Si. Nanoindentation measurements were performed at room temperature using a Berkovich indenter, with continuous stiffness measurements to 1500 nm at a strain rate of 0.05 s−1. Creep tests used a 15 mN peak load, 0.15 µN/s loading rate, and a 900 s hold, followed by a 120 s drift-correction segment at 10% load. Thus, this excerpt documents post-heat-treatment, room-temperature hardness/modulus and creep characterization; it does not provide hot-hardness measured at elevated temperature, phase-specific hot-stage observations, direct Al-alloy combinatorial additive-manufacturing data, or information on Singh (2026) and 316L.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide the original methods or results for Richter, Chen, and Smith (2008), so it cannot identify their specific Al–Ni–Si phases, test-temperature series, hot-hardness values, or creep observations. It does provide a closely related high-temperature nanoindentation methodology for Ni-base superalloys. Tests were conducted to 600°C in an environmental chamber purged with high-purity argon, with oxygen below 0.01% to limit oxidation. A heated diamond Berkovich tip was used below 500°C and a heated sapphire tip above 500°C because of diamond oxidation concerns. The specimens included solution-treated and aged single-crystal CMSX-4 oriented along <100> and <110>, plus a multicomponent diffusion multiple comprising Rene 95, IN718, IN100, and ME3. The diffusion multiple was examined both as-quenched and after an 1100°C, 8-hour exposure followed by furnace cooling, which coarsened intragranular γ′ precipitates. Hardness and modulus were mapped across graded interdiffusion zones. A 200 mN load, 3/9 mN/s loading/unloading rates, and 30–1500 s maximum-load dwells were used, providing an approach for assessing time-dependent (creep/viscoelastic) indentation behavior. No direct Al-alloy combinatorial-AM evidence or information about a 316L multi-specimen creep frame appears in this excerpt.

contexts.context: Kulkarni et al. (2023) directly demonstrate a high-throughput creep method for LPBF A205 aluminum alloy at 200 °C. Their approach is a small-scale cantilever bending creep test augmented by digital image correlation (DIC), which measures the two-dimensional strain field. The paper reports that one bending specimen/test can generate both tensile and compressive creep curves, making the method parallel in the sense of obtaining two loading-mode responses from a single test rather than running separate uniaxial experiments. The authors establish equivalence between bending-creep and conventional uniaxial-creep results. For solutionized-and-aged A205, creep-resistant behavior is reported at 120–180 MPa and 200 °C, with minimum strain rates on the order of 10^-8–10^-6 s^-1. The excerpt describes this as suitable for high-throughput data generation and structure–property evaluation. It does not report a composition library, combinatorial alloy screening, or parallel testing across multiple alloy compositions. It also contains no information about the HITEMAL/Krizik (2024) aluminum small-punch study, Singh et al. (2022) on AlSi10Mg, or Singh et al. contexts.context: The excerpt reports small-punch creep testing (SPCT) of an Al–Al₂O₃ composite, using ~0.5-mm-thick discs over 573–673 K and forces varied across many specimens (e.g., 69.7–158 N). Deflection–time curves showed primary, secondary, and tertiary creep, with fracture at 0.25–0.4 mm deflection. Time to fracture decreased exponentially with force. Data followed a Monkman–Grant relation, \(t_f=C_{MG}/\dot u_{\min}^{\alpha}\), with \(C_{MG}=1.003\), \(\alpha=0.834\), and \(R^2=0.987\). Transition forces were ~139, 133, and 109 N at 573, 623, and 673 K.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly documents Singh et al. (2026), rather than the cited Kulkarni et al. (2023), Krizik et al. (2024), or Singh et al. (2022) studies. Singh et al. introduce a simultaneous creep-testing method in which four specimens with different cross-sectional areas are connected in series. Because the specimens carry the same force but have different areas, they experience different stresses, while Digital Image Correlation independently measures their strain. The validation material is commercial 316 L stainless steel, using 1/5-scale ASTM-E8 pin-loaded specimens—not an aluminum alloy. Experiments were performed at 650 °C under nominal stresses of 250, 275, 300, and 325 MPa. The authors compared individual-specimen tests, used as benchmark measurements, with tests involving four coupled specimens. The assembly is tested until specimens fail sequentially; failed specimens are removed and testing resumes with the remaining specimens. The reported result is that the approach can perform up to four times as many creep tests within the same timeframe. This excerpt does not provide the requested explicit report about Singh et al. (2022)’s AlSi10Mg bending/DIC versus uniaxial equivalency at 250 °C and 75–140 MPa, nor does it describe Krizik et al. (2024)’s four small-punch discs and duplicate replicates at 573–673 K.

contexts.context: The supplied excerpt provides only partial information relevant to the requested comparison. For AM A205 (SA530WQ), Kulkarni et al. report that DIC-augmented bending creep and uniaxial tensile creep produce closely equivalent results: strain rates were identical below 170 MPa and differed by no more than a factor of two above 170 MPa. The bending tests covered approximately 120–180 MPa and produced minimum strain rates of 7 × 10⁻⁸ to 3 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹; the authors used the results to estimate a creep stress exponent of 6.5–7. However, this excerpt does not explicitly mention Singh et al. (2022), the reported 250 °C and 75–140 MPa AlSi10Mg bending-DIC conditions, or any page 2–3 discussion of that study. It also contains no information about Krizik et al. (2024), simultaneous testing of four small-punch discs, two replicates per condition, or temperatures of 573–673 K. Finally, it does not mention Singh et al. (2026), four specimens tested in series using 316L steel at 650 °C, or validation of those tests. Those claims therefore cannot be verified from the provided pages 5–7 excerpt.

contexts.context: Richter et al. (2008) report hot-stage nanoindentation of multi-component Al–Ni–Si piston alloys, measuring individual pure and intermetallic phases at room temperature, 500 K, and 650 K. They determined hardness and indentation modulus from load–displacement curves using Oliver–Pharr analysis, with AFM examining indents and FIB/TEM characterizing subsurface changes. Hardness and modulus decreased with temperature, while increasing Ni improved elevated-temperature mechanical stability. The study combines experiments with atomistic finite-element calculations, but concerns site-specific phase measurements rather than compositionally graded/additively manufactured libraries, creep tests, or explicitly high-throughput screening.

contexts.context: A 2024 study systematically tested one forged, powder-metallurgy UFG Al–Al₂O₃ composite stabilized by a continuous amorphous Al₂O₃ network. It used small-punch creep testing (SPCT) from 573–673 K and conventional tensile creep at 573 K, comparing results with Al alloys, Al–Al₄C₃/SiC composites, MP35N, and A2024-T81. SPCT produced reproducible minimum-deflection rates; tensile data showed superior creep resistance and longer fracture times. Reported stress exponents were 6.4–11.8 (low-stress) and 71–110 (high-stress). The excerpt describes focused specimen testing, not compositionally graded/combinatorial samples, hot hardness, nanoindentation, or multi-specimen high-throughput screening.

contexts.context: Richter et al. (2008) performed elevated-temperature instrumented nanoindentation on an Al–Ni–Si alloy, using indent rows across individual grains/phases and tracking composition by EDX/EBSD. They tested at 300, 500, and 650 K; grains were several tens of micrometers wide, enabling repeat indents and composition–hardness comparisons. At fixed load, penetration increased strongly with temperature and dwell-time creep. A 30-s dwell at 650 K was insufficient for complete creep relaxation. Plastic flow/creep differed between Al₇Cu₄Ni and Al₃Ni₂, with increased creep in Al₃Ni₂ at 650 K.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone screened aluminum alloys for elevated-temperature strength or creep resistance with high-throughput methods, for example hot hardness or high-temperature nanoindentation on compositionally graded or combinatorial additively manufactured samples, small-punch creep tests, or multi-specimen creep frames?

Yes. # High-throughput screening of aluminum alloys for hot strength and creep

**Yes—but the demonstrated approaches are mostly separate pieces of the proposed workflow.** Researchers have obtained multiple elevated-temperature creep curves from individual additively manufactured (AM) aluminum specimens, measured hot indentation properties locally within an aluminum alloy, and tested four aluminum-based small-punch creep specimens simultaneously. I did **not** find a published demonstration that combines a *compositionally graded AM aluminum-alloy library* with systematic hot-hardness mapping or long-duration creep screening across its compositions. That is a search-limited finding, not proof that no such study exists. (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 3-5, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 2-3, shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4, michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 1-3)

The table separates experiments that actually measured aluminum at elevated temperature from composition-library studies conducted at room temperature and multi-specimen methods demonstrated on other metals.

| Paper / method | Material and measured temperature | Actual throughput and evidence | Boundary of applicability |
|---|---|---|---|
| Singh et al. (2022), DIC-augmented cantilever creep | LPBF AlSi10Mg; **250 °C**, 75–140 MPa | One beam supplies creep data at multiple stress-invariant locations; reported good agreement with uniaxial creep (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3) | Direct elevated-temperature AM-Al demonstration, but details here come from Kulkarni et al.’s 2023 description rather than the inaccessible original; one alloy, not a composition library |
| Kulkarni et al. (2023), DIC-augmented cantilever creep | LPBF A205 (Al–Cu–Mg–Ag–TiB₂); **200 °C** | **Two cantilever tests** covered 120–180 MPa and generated tensile and compressive curves at multiple locations; rates matched conventional uniaxial results below 170 MPa and were within a factor of two above it (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3, kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 5-7) | Strong direct validation for rapid creep characterization of one AM alloy; not simultaneous screening of multiple compositions |
| Krizik et al. (2024), small-punch creep | HITEMAL ultrafine-grained Al–Al₂O₃ composite; **573–673 K (300–400 °C)** | Four loading stages permitted **four discs to be tested simultaneously**; 8-mm-diameter × 0.5-mm discs, two creep replicates per condition; correlated with tensile creep at 573 K (krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 1-3, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 3-5) | Direct parallel aluminum SPCT, but one material; converting punch force/deflection rate to uniaxial stress/rate requires material-specific calibration, and deformation localized near radial fractures |
| Richter et al. (2008), hot-stage nanoindentation | Multicomponent Al–Ni–Si piston alloy; **300, 500 and 650 K** | Repeated indents mapped local phases and a within-grain Ni variation; Al₃Ni₂, Al₇Cu₄Ni and Al₂Cu showed phase-dependent hardness loss and indentation creep (richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 1-2, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 2-3, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 4-5) | Direct hot hardness/local-creep evidence, but the specially coarsened specimen was neither an AM library nor a systematic combinatorial composition gradient |
| Shen et al. (2025), diffusion-multiple nanoindentation creep | **12 Al–Mg–Si micro-alloys** in a 6016/Al–3Si/Al–1.2Mg/Al diffusion multiple; measurements at **room temperature** | Three repeats per composition; 15-mN indentation with a **900-s hold** after diffusion annealing and solution/aging treatments (shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4) | Genuine high-throughput composition screening, but not elevated-temperature testing—the 530–540 °C steps fabricated/heat-treated the library rather than setting the indentation temperature |
| Singh et al. (2026), four specimens coupled in series with DIC | Commercial **316L stainless steel**, not aluminum; **650 °C**, 250–325 MPa | Four different cross-sections generated four stresses under one force; benchmarked against individual tests and delivered up to four creep tests in approximately the time of the slowest one (singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 1-3, singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 3-5, singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 10-11) | Demonstrates a transferable multi-specimen-frame concept, but provides no aluminum-alloy validation or compositional-library screen |


*Table: Direct and adjacent demonstrations are separated by whether they test aluminum at elevated temperature, multiplex specimens or stresses, or screen composition. The table also identifies important near-misses that should not be presented as hot combinatorial AM screening.*

**The closest AM-aluminum creep-screening examples are DIC-instrumented cantilever tests.** Kulkarni and colleagues performed two bending-creep tests on LPBF A205 at **200 °C**. Different stress-invariant positions along each beam, on both its tensile and compressive sides, supplied creep responses spanning **120–180 MPa**. Their minimum creep rates agreed with conventional uniaxial results below **170 MPa** and were within a factor of two above that stress. Thus, “high throughput” here means *multiple stress and loading-mode measurements per specimen*, not multiple alloy compositions tested concurrently. The paper also reports that an earlier study by Singh and colleagues found bending–uniaxial agreement for LPBF AlSi10Mg at **250 °C and 75–140 MPa**; I could verify those particulars in Kulkarni’s paper but could not inspect the original Singh article. Kulkarni’s Figure 5(a) directly compares the bending and uniaxial minimum-rate measurements. (kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 2-3, kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof pages 5-7, kulkarni2023creepbehaviorof media 6a17e918)

**Actual parallel aluminum small-punch creep testing has also been demonstrated.** Krizik and colleagues tested a powder-metallurgy, oxide-network-strengthened Al–Al₂O₃ material (HITEMAL) at **573–673 K (300–400 °C)**. Their furnace had **four independently loaded measurement cells**, allowing four **8-mm-diameter, approximately 0.5-mm-thick discs** to run simultaneously; they tested two creep specimens per condition. They compared punch results with conventional tensile creep at **573 K** and proposed a material-specific stress correlation. This is substantive parallel testing, but of one aluminum-based composite rather than a graded alloy library. Punch force and deflection rate do not directly equal uniaxial stress and strain rate, and the discs fractured after relatively small, localized deformation—important constraints on ranking alloys from punch results alone. (krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 1-3, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 3-5, krizik2024creeppropertiesof pages 5-7)

**Hot indentation and combinatorial composition screening have been shown separately.** Richter and colleagues indented individual phases and local Ni variations in an Al–Ni–Si piston alloy at **300, 500 and 650 K**, finding phase-dependent hot-hardness loss and indentation creep. This was a phase-resolved study of a specially prepared alloy, **not** a combinatorial AM build. Conversely, Shen and colleagues made a diffusion multiple containing **12 sampled Al–Mg–Si micro-alloy compositions** and measured hardness and 900-s indentation creep across it, but the *measurements were at room temperature*. Its high-temperature diffusion and aging steps must not be mistaken for hot indentation tests. (richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 1-2, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 2-3, richter2008hotstagenanoindentation pages 4-5, shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4)

Finally, a **four-specimen, single-frame tensile-creep** design with separate DIC strain measurements has been validated at **650 °C**, but its demonstration material was **316L stainless steel, not aluminum**. It establishes a plausible apparatus strategy, not an aluminum-screening precedent. Overall, the literature supports a workflow in which combinatorial aluminum fabrication is followed by rapid local screening and then calibrated bending or parallel small-punch creep tests. The remaining evidentiary gap is a demonstrated, composition-resolved *elevated-temperature* aluminum screen that establishes how its rapid measurements predict conventional long-term creep performance. (singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 1-3, singh2026anovelhighthroughput pages 3-5, michi2022towardshightemperatureapplications pages 1-3, shen2025highthroughputstudyon pages 2-4)
